What moves the stocks week to week

Each stock's weekly euro return is regressed on the STOXX Europe 600, the change in EUR/USD and the Hang Seng index (Newey–West standard errors). Dots show the estimated sensitivity (beta); bars are 95% intervals; filled dots are significant at the 5% level.

Table view: full-sample regression results
Market β EUR/USD β China β t (mkt) t (FX) t (China) R²
LVMH 1.07 0.29 0.08 10.83 2.24 1.46 0.46
Hermès 0.83 0.19 0.10 9.68 1.42 1.99 0.33
Kering 1.11 0.38 0.20 11.93 2.57 3.00 0.37
Richemont 1.07 0.22 0.22 11.32 1.44 3.34 0.43
Moncler 0.99 0.36 0.10 8.83 2.26 1.62 0.30
Burberry 1.15 -0.04 0.22 11.92 -0.26 2.87 0.33
Prada 0.65 -0.30 0.41 6.87 -1.48 4.42 0.17
Brunello Cucinelli 0.91 0.41 0.06 7.23 2.68 0.77 0.23
  • The market dominates, yet explains less than half. R² ranges from 17% to 46%.
  • A stronger euro has not hurt luxury stocks week to week. The EUR/USD beta is positive for most names, the opposite of the translation-effect hypothesis. A weak dollar tends to coincide with global risk appetite; the accounting hit from translation shows up in reported earnings, over quarters.
  • China matters beyond the market for Hermès, Kering, Richemont, Burberry and Prada (Hermès only marginally). With the MSCI China ETF as the proxy, 7 of 8 are significant.

Luxury became more market-sensitive after 2022 and less tied to Chinese equities, which peaked in 2020–22. Part of the rise in market beta may be mechanical: LVMH, Hermès and Richemont are large constituents of the STOXX 600 itself.

Reading tip: a step that reverses exactly two years later is one extreme week entering and then leaving the window, not a lasting change. The clearest case is March 2020, when the STOXX 600 fell 20% in a week.

Since 2023: a sector shock or a brand problem?

Factor sensitivities are estimated on 2014–2022 only, then used to predict 2023–2026 returns. The gap between actual and predicted returns is split into the part shared with the other seven luxury stocks and the brand-specific remainder.

Table view: cumulative log points since January 2023

Richemont 3 -40 43
Moncler -46 -50 4
Burberry -107 -28 -78
Prada -40 -44 4
Brunello Cucinelli -13 -41 28
  • Every name carries a sector-wide drag (median −37 log points): the slowdown hit luxury as a whole.
  • On top of that, brands diverge sharply: Kering at −100 points brand-specific, Richemont at +43.
  • Read the brand split as relative. Each stock is compared with the average of the other seven, so one peer's collapse makes the others look stronger.

  • Reactions are large only where the brand dominates group profit: Demna at Gucci and Tisci at Burberry. LVMH appointments (Louis Vuitton, Dior) barely register.
  • At Kering, CEO changes moved the stock more than most creative changes, but there are only four of them, at a company in turnaround.
  • Few results survive multiple testing. With 20 events and several windows, a handful of significant results is expected by chance; only the largest, such as Demna at |t| ≈ 6, are robust.

Data and method

  • Prices: Yahoo Finance via yfinance (adjusted close; raw data not redistributed). Indices: STOXX Europe 600, Hang Seng, iShares MSCI China ETF.
  • FX: ECB euro reference rates (USD, CHF, GBP, HKD); all stocks converted to EUR.
  • Returns: Friday-to-Friday log returns, which limit distortions from markets closing at different times; daily returns for the event study, aligned on common trading days.
  • Validation: no missing weeks; no stale prices; extreme moves flagged for review (partly checked against news); Yahoo's STOXX 600 lacks 64 trading days since 2014, handled by aligning prices before computing returns.
  • Events: each date verified against press coverage, with timing and confounders recorded.

Limitations

  • Associations, not causal effects. Weekly co-movement says nothing about fundamental exposure.
  • The European market index contains several of the stocks studied.
  • Brand-specific gaps are relative to peers, and the 2014–22 benchmark assumes stable sensitivities.
  • Event study: small sample, possible leaks before announcements, and same-day news (e.g. COVID on 24 Feb 2020; the Hang Seng crash on 8 Oct 2024).
